(3) Prompts bypass scored retrieval exactly as described: diary uses raw for_day()/summaries() slices (cognition/narrative.py:89-90) and reflect uses an importance-only sort of for_day() (narrative.py:101-107) — never retrieve(), so recency decay and embedding relevance never influence any prompt, despite README.md:90 advertising "recency/importance/relevance retrieval". (4) AgentState.memory is built via field(default_factory=MemoryStream) (agents/agent.py:44) and build_world (kernel/kernel.py:32-53) never passes memory config; grep confirms alpha_recency/beta_importance/gamma_relevance/recency_decay_per_tick/retrieve_k appear only in config/models.py:100-104 (and as independent same-named defaults in memory.py:34-37 — config field recency_decay_per_tick does not even share a name with MemoryStream.decay_per_tick), so changing them in townsim.yaml has no effect. The claim correctly excludes compact_after_days (models.py:105), which IS wired (kernel.py:126). Execution-path check: default_systems() (systems.py:411-413) and Kernel.step (kernel.py:76-104) plus day rollover (kernel.py:107-136) never reach retrieve() or embed(). Severity Minor is correct: dead code and misleading configuration, no runtime fault.

findings.title: flush_intents stamps events with a tick that was never stepped
findings.description: flush_intents builds its SysContext with clock.at(self.tick) (kernel.py:213-214), but step() increments self.tick before returning (kernel.py:104), so self.tick always refers to the NEXT, not-yet-executed tick. In strict mode the rollover flush therefore journals schedule_override_applied / reflection_applied / diary_written at tick T+1 before tick T+1's own step events, and the end-of-run flush in run_kernel's finally block (loop.py:56) stamps events with a tick that never executes at all, so the journal's last records lie about when they happened (their MemoryEntry.tick recency values are similarly skewed). It is still deterministic (same wrong tick every run), so the hash is unaffected; the defect is journal/timestamp accuracy for replay analysis.
findings.fix: Use clock.at(max(0, self.tick - 1)) in flush_intents (the tick whose boundary the intents are being applied at), or record an explicit 'applied_at_boundary_of' field instead of borrowing the next tick's timestamp.

verdict.justification: Traced and confirmed. step() computes now = clock.at(self.tick) at kernel.py:77 and increments self.tick at kernel.py:103 before returning, so after stepping tick T, self.tick == T+1. flush_intents (kernel.py:209-216) builds SysContext with now=self.clock.at(self.tick) at kernel.py:212-213, and SysContext.emit (townsim/systems.py:38-40) stamps Event.tick/day_index from that now — so all flush-applied events (schedule_override_applied, reflection_applied, diary_written at kernel.py:160/186/193) carry tick T+1. In strict mode (loop.py:36-39) these are journaled via kernel.py:215 immediately after the rollover step T and before tick T+1's own step events (journaled at kernel.py:101); at the final rollover the loop breaks at loop.py:45 right after the flush, and the non-strict end-of-run flush in the finally block (loop.py:56) runs after the loop ends, so in both terminal cases the stamped tick (and its day_index, computed by SimClock.at) never executes. MemoryEntry.tick skew also confirmed at kernel.py:191-192 and 204 (ctx.now.tick in flush context). The finding's mitigating claims also check out: schedule_override_applied is BEHAVIORAL (events.py:18) and hashed (journal.py:36-37), but the wrong stamp is identical across runs, so test_strict_mode_full_loop_reproducible (tests/test_simulation.py:52-60) passes; no test asserts the tick stamp of flushed events, so the passing suite does not contradict the claim. Minor caveats that do not rise to PARTIAL: the cited line numbers are off by one (increment at 103 not 104; SysContext at 212-213), and for mid-run strict rollovers the T+1 stamp is arguably a defensible boundary convention since tick T+1 is subsequently stepped and the effects first become visible then — but the end-of-run/final-rollover stamps genuinely reference never-executed sim times, and the same boundary application is stamped inconsistently between the in-step path (kernel.py:92, current tick) and the flush path (next tick). Impact is correctly scoped to journal/timestamp accuracy with no behavioral or hash effect; Minor is the right severity.

findings.title: ws_endpoint leaks registered sockets on non-WebSocketDisconnect exits: hub.connect outside try, only WebSocketDisconnect caught
findings.description: Two traced paths never call hub.disconnect: (1) `await hub.connect(ws, kernel)` (app.py:101) is OUTSIDE the try block — if the client closes between accept and the init send (common on rapid refresh), `_send` raises after the socket was already added to hub._clients (hub.py:28-30), the exception propagates to uvicorn ('Exception in ASGI application' noise), and the dead socket stays registered. (2) Inside the loop only WebSocketDisconnect is caught (app.py:115); with installed starlette 1.3.1, `receive_text` on a client-sent BINARY frame returns message['bytes'] and `message["text"]` raises KeyError — endpoint dies without cleanup. Stale sockets are normally self-culled by the next broadcast's per-client except (hub.py:91-96), but while `kernel.paused` is true run_kernel never calls on_tick (loop.py:28-30), so no broadcast runs and dead sockets accumulate in hub._clients for as long as the sim stays paused (unbounded with a flapping/reconnecting client); they are only purged after resume.
findings.fix: Restructure the endpoint as: try: await hub.connect(...); while True: ... except WebSocketDisconnect: pass; finally: await hub.disconnect(ws). Optionally catch Exception around the receive loop body and use receive_json/receive with type checks so binary frames don't raise KeyError.

verdict.justification: Both leak paths were verified by static trace and empirical reproduction against the real app with the installed dependencies (starlette 1.3.1, uvicorn 0.50.0, fastapi 0.139.0). (1) townsim/server/app.py:101 calls `await hub.connect(ws, kernel)` OUTSIDE the try block starting at line 102; hub.connect (townsim/server/hub.py:27-30) adds the socket to `_clients` (line 29) before sending the init payload (line 30). If the client closes between accept and that send, uvicorn's websockets_sansio_impl raises ClientDisconnected (OSError subclass, uvicorn/protocols/utils.py:10; websockets_sansio_impl.py:455-456), which starlette converts to WebSocketDisconnect(1006) (starlette/websockets.py:85-89) — raised before the try, so the `except WebSocketDisconnect` at app.py:115 never applies, hub.disconnect is never called, and uvicorn's run_asgi logs "Exception in ASGI application" (websockets_sansio_impl.py:345-352, which special-cases only ClientDisconnected, not WebSocketDisconnect). (2) A client-sent binary frame arrives as {"type":"websocket.receive","bytes":...} with no "text" key (websockets_sansio_impl.py:250 — the auto-selected protocol per auto.py), so starlette receive_text's `message["text"]` (starlette/websockets.py:121) raises KeyError, which escapes the WebSocketDisconnect-only except and leaks the socket. Empirical harness driving the real create_app() ASGI app reproduced both: control client cleans up (_clients=0), path 1 leaks 1 socket (WebSocketDisconnect escapes), path 2 leaks another (KeyError escapes). The paused-accumulation clause is also correct: townsim/kernel/loop.py:28-30 sleeps and continues without calling on_tick while kernel.paused, so the broadcast self-culling in hub.py:87-96 never runs during pause; dead sockets accumulate until resume or a pause/resume broadcast from another client. No test in tests/ touches the websocket endpoint or hub, so the 65 passing tests do not contradict the finding. Only trivial imprecision: the phrase "returns message['bytes']" is garbled wording, but the operative mechanism (KeyError on message["text"]) is exactly what happens. Minor severity is appropriate (self-healing after resume; log noise plus bounded-by-client-flapping memory growth).

findings.title: load_config silently ignores an explicit --config path that does not exist
findings.description: When yaml_path is given, candidates = [Path(yaml_path)] only; if that file is missing, the for-loop finds nothing, `data` stays {}, and SimConfig is built from hard-coded defaults - with no error and no fallback to default.yaml. Execution path: `python -m townsim run --config prod.yml` (typo for prod.yaml) -> cli.cmd_run -> load_config('prod.yml') -> runs an entire simulation with default seed/provider/needs while the user believes their config applied. For a research tool whose selling point is reproducible, configured runs, a silently-dropped config file corrupts experiments.
findings.fix: If yaml_path was explicitly provided and does not exist, raise FileNotFoundError (or at least log a prominent warning) instead of falling through to defaults.

verdict.justification: Verified in code and empirically. townsim/config/models.py:123 sets candidates=[Path(yaml_path)] when an explicit path is given — no fallback entries; the loop (lines 128-132) only loads a candidate if it exists, so a missing file leaves data={} (line 127) and line 133 returns SimConfig(**{}) built from hard-coded defaults with no error or warning. The claimed execution path exists exactly: cli.py:111 defines --config, cli.py:65 (cmd_run) and cli.py:51 (cmd_serve) call load_config(args.config) with no existence check. Empirical test with the project venv: load_config('does_not_exist_prod.yml') raised nothing and returned seed=42, provider=auto — pure defaults. No test contradicts: grep shows load_config is referenced only by cli.py and the config package itself; none of the 65 passing tests cover the missing-explicit-path case. Only immaterial nuance: TOWNSIM_* env vars and CLI flags still apply (SimConfig is a BaseSettings), so a run isn't strictly all-defaults if those are set — but the explicitly requested YAML is silently ignored exactly as described. Severity Minor is appropriate.

findings.title: Test suite inherits ambient TOWNSIM_* environment variables, breaking test isolation
findings.description: The `cfg` fixture builds `SimConfig()` - a BaseSettings subclass that reads real TOWNSIM_* env vars - and only pins seed, ticks_per_second, strict_narrative_sync, provider, and runs_dir afterwards. Everything else (kernel.tick_minutes, day_start_hour, needs rates/thresholds, interaction knobs, paths.map_file, memory settings) remains env-controlled. README.md explicitly encourages exporting vars like TOWNSIM_KERNEL__SEED / TOWNSIM_LLM__PROVIDER; a developer with e.g. TOWNSIM_KERNEL__TICK_MINUTES=5 or TOWNSIM_NEEDS__HUNGER_CRITICAL=50 exported gets different sim dynamics and flaky/failing determinism and integration tests (test_schedule's clock tests construct SimClock directly, but test_simulation, test_content:14 and test_pathfinding:10 all go through SimConfig()). The failure will look like a nondeterministic regression rather than an env problem.
findings.fix: In conftest.py, add an autouse fixture that strips TOWNSIM_* from os.environ (monkeypatch.delenv for each matching key) before constructing SimConfig, or construct the test config with explicit values (SimConfig.model_construct or a plain dict) instead of the env-reading constructor.

verdict.justification: Empirically reproduced. tests/conftest.py:10 constructs SimConfig(), which is a pydantic BaseSettings with env_prefix="TOWNSIM_" and env_nested_delimiter="__" (townsim/config/models.py:108-109), then pins only seed, ticks_per_second, strict_narrative_sync, llm.provider, and paths.runs_dir (conftest.py:11-15). No test or fixture strips TOWNSIM_* vars (no monkeypatch/delenv anywhere in tests/; no pytest-env in pyproject.toml), and tests/test_pathfinding.py:10 and tests/test_content.py:18 call SimConfig() directly. README.md:40 documents exporting TOWNSIM_* vars as the normal override workflow. Reproduction: baseline suite passes 65/65; with TOWNSIM_KERNEL__TICK_MINUTES=5 exported, SimConfig() inside the test process returns tick_minutes=5 (leak confirmed, suite happened to still pass); with TOWNSIM_NEEDS__HUNGER_RATE=2.0 exported, tests/test_simulation.py::TestTwoDayRun::test_full_pipeline fails (1 failed, 64 passed) via its starvation assertion — presenting as a sim regression rather than an env problem, exactly as claimed. Minor peripheral inaccuracies that do not change the verdict: the two README-named examples (TOWNSIM_KERNEL__SEED, TOWNSIM_LLM__PROVIDER) are re-pinned by the fixture and thus harmless; the within-suite determinism tests (test_same_seed_same_hash) do not fail under a constant env var since both kernels share the same environment; and the test_content citation is line 18, not 14. The core defect — test suite inherits ambient TOWNSIM_* environment and integration tests fail under plausibly-exported overrides — is demonstrably real. Severity Minor is appropriate (test-hygiene issue, no product-code defect).

findings.title: Determinism tests leak open journal file handles when the assertion fails (Windows tmp_path cleanup hazard)
findings.description: test_same_seed_same_hash and test_different_seed_different_hash call `k1.close(), k2.close()` AFTER the hash assertion. Each Kernel opens runs_dir/journal.jsonl in append mode at construction (townsim/kernel/journal.py:24). If the determinism assertion ever fails (exactly the scenario these tests exist to catch), close() is never reached and two file handles into pytest's tmp_path stay open until garbage collection; on Windows this can make tmp_path teardown/retention cleanup fail with PermissionError noise that buries the real determinism failure. The async tests are safe only because run_kernel's finally block closes the kernel (townsim/kernel/loop.py:59).
findings.fix: Wrap the body in try/finally (close both kernels before asserting, or assert inside try and close in finally), or make the tests use `contextlib.closing`/a small fixture that guarantees kernel.close(). Adding Kernel.__enter__/__exit__ would make this idiomatic everywhere.

verdict.justification: The leak itself is CONFIRMED: tests/test_simulation.py:40-41 and :49-50 call k1.close(), k2.close() only after the hash assert, Kernel.__init__ opens the journal handle at construction (townsim/kernel/kernel.py:67 -> townsim/kernel/journal.py:24, open(..., "a")), the file lives under pytest tmp_path (tests/conftest.py:15), and only the async tests are protected by run_kernel's finally (townsim/kernel/loop.py:53-59). Empirically verified on Windows that the open handle blocks rmtree with PermissionError WinError 32. However, the claimed consequence — "tmp_path teardown/retention cleanup fail with PermissionError noise that buries the real determinism failure" — is refuted for this repo: pyproject.toml sets no tmp_path_retention_policy, and installed pytest 9.1.1 defaults to "all" (.venv/.../_pytest/tmpdir.py:271), under which pytest never deletes the current session's tmp dirs in-process; deletion happens only under policy "failed" AND a passing test (tmpdir.py:303-310) or passing session (tmpdir.py:315-333) — a failed determinism test's dir is always retained except under "none". Moreover every pytest cleanup path uses rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True) or swallows OSError (source comments explicitly cite "leaked resource ... we ignore it"), so no PermissionError noise can surface, and prior-session pruning runs in a later process after the OS has closed the leaked handles. Net: real test-hygiene defect (non-exception-safe cleanup; the suggested try/finally fix is apt), misdescribed impact. Severity remains Minor, the floor of the scale.
